y1-micro1.name: Micro 1: Principles
y1-micro1.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The goal of the course is to introduce students to the most important concepts and tools of microeconomic analysis. Students will be equipped with an analytic toolbox to solve microeconomic problems and will be trained in interpreting microeconomic issues. On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Find the market equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market and recognize factors that influence demand, supply, and market equilibrium. Analyze how a consumer chooses between different bundles of goods; how a firm chooses between different inputs; and evaluate factors that influence these choices. Calculate and analyze short- and long-run market outcomes (such as equilibrium price, elasticities, consumer surplus, producer surplus) in perfectly competitive markets. Analyze the effects of different forms of government intervention (such as taxes, subsidies, and price regulation) on market outcomes. Calculate and analyze market outcomes when firms have market power (monopoly) and calculate and analyze how this affects the welfare of consumers and producers.
y1-micro1.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Economics is about the allocation of scarce resources. Who gets what share of the resources depends on the actions taken by the economic agents involved. Amongst others, there are consumers, workers, managers, labor unions, firms, and governmental bodies involved. Understanding how economic agents make their decisions is the foundation of understanding how economics work. Microeconomics is about the economic behavior of individual economic decision-makers. Examples of the questions covered here are: "How do consumers divide up their restricted budget to buy different goods?", "How do workers divide their restricted time between labor and leisure?", "How do firms optimize their production process, minimize their cost, and maximize their profits?" Microeconomics is also about the interaction of economic agents. It analyses the effects of the decisions of one agent on the decision-making of others. Amongst the questions studied here are "How are individual consumers' decisions aggregated to create market demand?", "How are firms' decisions aggregated to create market supply?", "How do consumers and firms react when the government changes taxation?" In this course, we build up the basics of microeconomic theory in three blocks. First, we discuss the theory of consumer choice, then the focus is shifted towards the theory of firm behavior and finally, we analyze product markets in which consumers and producers meet and the government can intervene. Type of instructions All lectures will be pre-recorded in video clips. These video clips will introduce the concepts and toolboxes. In addition, every week, there will be an on-campus Q&A lecture with discussions about the video clips of the week. On top of lectures, there will be weekly tutorials. The main purpose of the tutorials is that the student can apply the concepts learned in the lectures to specific problems. Microeconomics is not a 'learning by heart' topic, but a "learning by doing" topic, so solving specific problem sets and interpreting results is a large part of the material. The students will be asked to prepare some exercises before tutorial meetings, which will be discussed and extended during the tutorial. In each tutorial there will be a graded quiz based on the exercises that are shared with the students before the tutorial. The grade of the quizzes determines the participation grade. Active participation in both Q&A lectures and tutorials is required and highly appreciated. Tutorials will be done on-campus. Compulsory Reading Besanko, David A. and Ronald R. Braeutigam, Microeconomics - 5th edition , John Wiley and Sons, New York, 2015, ISBN 9781118716380. The 4th edition of the book (2011) is also fine. All additional material covered in classes

y1-macro1.name: Macro 1: Principles
y1-macro1.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After completion of this course the students should understand how microeconomics differs from macroeconomics and they should be familiar with important macroeconomic facts, problems, and basic macroeconomic theories. More specifically, they can: Describe, interpret and apply specific macroeconomic concepts. Explain the general concept of economic modelling. Analyse and interpret important macroeconomic facts, problems, and link them to basic macroeconomic theories. Analyze numerically and graphically how macroeconomic policies and shocks affect a closed and open economy in the long run. Analyze numerically and graphically how macroeconomic policies and shocks affect an closed economy in the short run. Debate macroeconomic problems in a group.
y1-macro1.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In the first part of the course, the students learn the basic mathematical and graphical tools used for macroeconomic analysis and they learn how macroeconomics relates to microeconomics. Subsequently, they learn determinants of long-run economic output, average inflation, and structural unemployment, as well as their measurement. Concluding this first part, the students learn some aspects of international economics, such as how exchange rates, capital flows between countries, and the trade balance are affected by policies and shocks. In the second part of the course, recessions and booms are studied, where business cycles are understood as short-run deviations of economic activity around the long-run levels determined in the first part. Students learn how macroeconomic policies and shocks affect economic output, employment and interest rates in the short run in case of a closed economy. All parts discuss to what extent governments and central banks can influence the economy using fiscal, monetary and other types of policy. At the end of the course, the students participate in a role play about macroeconomic policies.

y1-math.name: Mathematics
y1-math.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Recognize economic problems as mathematical problems and provides mathematical tools for solving these problems. report a calculation or reasoning in a structured way. Report a calculation or reasoning in a structured way
y1-math.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The following subjects will be discussed: Functions of one variable Functions of more than one variable Convexity and concavity of functions Derivatives and differentials Optimization: Unconstrained optimization Constrained optimization Integration Various applications of the mathematical notions mentioned above in economics. Type of instructions 3 hours lecture during 14 weeks and 2 hours tutorial during 7 weeks. Please note, that this course is only open to students of the Economics program and cannot be used as an elective for other programs.

y1-accounting.name: Accounting
y1-accounting.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Explore fundamental accounting concepts, theories and metaphors (e.g., double-entry bookkeeping, financial statements, costs, accounting principles, accounting as the language of business, accountability, control) – the “what” of accounting Apply accounting techniques (e.g., journal entries, accounting cycle, costing methods, control systems) – the “how” of accounting Give real-world examples of the use accounting concepts, theories, metaphors and techniques – the “where” of accounting Inquire on the social and moral ramification of accounting language and accounting thinking – the “why” of accounting
y1-accounting.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In their 2020 article titled “ It’s 2020: What is Accounting Today? ”, authors Garry Carnegie, Lee Parker and Eva Tsahuridu expand the definition of accounting as a “technical, social and moral practice concerned with the sustainable utilisation of resources and proper accountability to stakeholders to enable the flourishing of organisations, people and nature.”. In this course we will explore accounting through its expanded definition. This means we will examine the language of accounting not only from a technical perspective – which includes financial accounting, management accounting and accounting information systems concepts and metaphors – but also from a moral, social and flourishing perspective. At its core, this course aims to broaden your vocabulary to include the language of accounting. In terms of content, this course will build on the technical terminology of financial statements, transactions, accounting systems and processes, costing methods, performance metrics and decision-making. However, through the course activities, we will also explore the idea that context – not just numbers – plays a crucial role in how the language of accounting is understood and interpreted.

y1-philosophy.name: Philosophy, Science and Free Markets
y1-philosophy.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } PART 1: After the successful completion of this part of the course, students can Explain common reasoning errors, why we make them, what they lead to (domains of irrationality), why that matters, and how the scientific method and context protect against common reasoning errors. Apply critical thinking in everyday and economic contexts. PART 2: After the successful completion of this part of the course, students can: Explain and apply influential philosophical theories about distributive justice. Explain and apply influential philosophical theories on the place of the market in a just society. Develop coherent and convincing arguments for normative positions and constructively evaluate the arguments of other students.
y1-philosophy.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Assessment Part 1 - Philosophy of science Consists of a written exam and a writing assignment. 4.1. Exam The midterm exam counts for 70% of the final mark for Philosophy of science. The midterm exam consists of 4 open questions. The exam material consists of all required readings as well as everything discussed in the lectures and tutorials (take notes!). A resit exam will be organized (look at the exam schedule for details). 4.2. Writing assignment The remaining 30% of the final mark will be determined by the individual writing assignment. The assignment will be announced during a lecture and posted on Blackboard. A resit opportunity for the assignment will be offered. Deadline assignment: Friday October 5 th 2018 (17h30). Deadline resit assignment: Monday January 21st 2019 (17h30). part 2 - Philosophy of Free Markets This part of the course is examined by a final exam and a writing assignment. 4.1. The final exam The final exam determines 70 percent of the final mark of this part. It will consist of open questions and multiple choice questions. The required material for the final exam consists of all required literature and all lectures (i.e., lecture notes). The final exam can be retaken (check the exam schedule for details). 4.2. The writing assignment The writing assignment determines 30 percent of the final mark of this part. The assignment will be issued during the first tutorial and on Blackboard. The deadline for submission of the assignment is December 7 th 2018 (5.30 pm) . The tutorials will help students to fulfil the assignment. In particular, students will be able to receive feedback during tutorial 3. There is a resit for the writing assignment. The resit deadline is January 21 st 2019 (5.30 pm).

y1-micro2.name: Micro 2: Welfare Economics
y1-micro2.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Central issue in this course is why the government should have a role in the economy - and how different policy instruments affect social welfare. On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 1. Evaluate the rationale for government intervention in the economy by analyzing market failures, public goods, and externalities. 2. Analyze the impact of various policy instruments on economic efficiency, equity, and social welfare. 3. Assess different economic policy approaches in real-world contexts, considering their trade-offs and effectiveness in addressing societal challenges. 4. Collect and organize information on policy instruments from academic papers and news outlets. 5. Using a presentation, explain the pros and cons of different real-world policy approaches to a broad audience in a clear and effective way.
y1-micro2.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In microeconomics 1, you learned how markets work. Now, in microeconomics 2, you learn why markets sometimes fail, and what to do in that case. In particular, we discuss what the government can do about it, and why the government will also likely to fail in some situations. We discuss five rationales for government intervention: (1) externalities; (2) public goods (and public interest goods); (3) paternalistic motives; (4) market structuring and market regulation, and (5) redistribution. We provide you with the tools to assess alternative policies that are aimed at correcting inefficient and unfair market outcomes. To closely connect the course to issues in the real world, we frequently use examples and case studies. Type of instructions Lectures and tutorials Required Prerequisites Microeconomics 1 (semester 1)

y1-macro2.name: Macro 2: International Finance
y1-macro2.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } This course is to be regarded as an introduction to the world of international finance. After attending this course, students will have an insight into the standard theories of exchange rate determination as well as of international macro-economic policy making, including their empirical applications. On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: - identify the determinants of the exchange rates, - list the main modern and historical monetary systems, - explain the effects of macroeconomic policy in open economies, - interpret the effectiveness of monetary and fiscal policy under different exchange rate regimes, - put together the theoretical frameworks and the empirical evidence to evaluate the causes and consequences of contemporary macro-economic phenomena such as global imbalances Please note that this course is only open to students of the Economics program and cannot be used as an elective for other programs.
y1-macro2.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In the first part of the course, the theoretical frameworks, which are utilized to understand the relationship between exchange rates, interest rates, price levels and product market developments, both in the short and in the long run, and both under flexible and under fixed exchange rates, are presented. In the second part, these models are applied to actual cases of international macroeconomic policy making. Topics to be addressed include macroeconomic policy and international coordination under floating exchange rates, optimum currency areas, the European experience (EMU) and international financial markets. Type of instructions Lectures and tutorials

y1-finance.name: Finance & Investment
y1-finance.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After successful completion of the course, students will be able to Identify, explain and apply fundamental financial concepts and theory (such as Time Value of Money, Law of One Price, Capital Budgeting Decision Rules, the Capital Asset Pricing Model, and Cost of Capital) Assess whether an investment is worthwhile, how it might be improved, and be funded Compare and discuss asset pricing and corporate finance topics and their interaction (at an introductory level) Formulate sound financial advice leveraging concepts in CG1
y1-finance.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The central themes in this introductory course are cash flow analysis, the time value of money, the risk-return relationship, and investments. More specifically, the following topics will be dealt with: Financial Decision Making and Law of One Price Time Value of Money & Interest Rates Investment Decision Rules Bond and Stock Valuation Risk/Return Trade-offs Portfolio Theory Capital Asset Pricing Model Estimating Cost of Capital Market Efficiency and Investor Behavior

y1-statistics.name: Statistics
y1-statistics.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Explain and apply fundamental probability concepts and rules, such as random variables, probability distributions, probability density functions, and cumulative distribution functions, to solve basic probability problems in economic and real-world situations. Calculate and interpret probabilities and important measures of random variables, such as expectations, variances, and relationships between variables, using different types of distributions and statistical tables, and apply these skills to real-world data. Describe and visualize quantitative and qualitative data using graphical methods and descriptive statistics such as mean, median, cumulative distributions, histograms for economic and empirical data sets. Estimate, test, and interpret population parameters using sample data by constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests, and evaluate results in applied economic and decision-making contexts. Perform and interpret probability and statistical analyses using statistical software, particularly Excel (and basic R), to analyze, summarize, and draw conclusions from real-world economic data.
y1-statistics.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } This course provides a statistical basis that can be used in other courses both in the first year and in later years of the study program. The course treats the following subjects: Descriptive statistics (population and sample statistics, graphs) Probability theory (the classical definition of probability, probability rules) Random variables, probability distributions, probability density functions Expectation, variance, standard deviation, covariance, correlation Sampling theory, random samples Estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. Relation with other courses The methods and techniques learned in this course will be applied in other courses. We specifically mention Econometrics for ECO (which uses this course as a starting point, extends the notions and develops regression theory), Micro 3: Game Theory (probability theory) and the elective Experimental and Behaviorial Economics (continues on analyzing data and testing). Please note, that this course is only open to students of the Economics program and cannot be used as an elective for other programs.

y1-r.name: Programming in R
y1-r.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: work with RStudio; being able to write simple programs in R, say to declare (collections of) variables, plot a function, make a histogram. use more advanced tools in R, like optimizing a function, finding roots of a function, using flow control and selection statements, reading data files, creating dataframes, merging dataframes, going from wide to long form. "predict" the outcome of running a cell with R code, being able to interpret such output, and being able to find solutions to errors. simulate stochastic/economic models, to collect information and to give an intuition for the results.
y1-r.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } R is a very popular open-source programming language which is dedicated to data analysis and statistics. When you have finished this course, you should feel comfortable using a computer and modern, powerful open-source software. The ultimate goal of this course is to make sure that all students, regardless of their affinity with computers coming in to this course, can either solve simple problems themselves or know how to find a solution (online). To achieve this, students learn to create notebooks and write texts in markdown. Students learn elementary programming concepts (loops, data structures, dataframes, ...) in R. Students will be able to analyze data, report analyses using graphs or use simulations to explain difficult concepts to a non-technical audience (say, your future employer and colleagues). Notebooks allow you to combine code with text to explain what you are doing. This makes it easy to reproduce your research. Moreover, it allows you to explain the economics and econometrics that you use to people who do not necessarily have a background in economics. For students with little or no background in programming this course may seem daunting. This course is developed in such a way that every student, who puts some effort into it, will acquire basic programming skills. This course creates a level playing field, in terms of computer skills, in anticipation of more advanced courses using R and other software. Type of instructions Interactive tutorials and some lectures Type of exams Computer exam

y1-python.name: Programming in Python
y1-python.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: work with Jupyter notebooks; being able to write simple programs in Python, say to declare (collections of) variables, plot a function, make a histogram. use more advanced tools in Python, like optimizing a function, finding roots of a function, using flow control and selection statements, reading data files, creating dataframes, merging dataframes, going from wide to long form. "predict" the outcome of running a cell with Python code, being able to interpret such output, and being able to find solutions to errors. simulate stochastic/economic models, to collect information and to give an intuition for the results.

When you have finished this course, you should feel comfortable using a computer and modern, powerful open-source software. The ultimate goal of this course is to make sure that all students, regardless of their affinity with computers coming in to this course, can either solve simple problems themselves or know how to find a solution (online). To achieve this, students learn to create notebooks and write texts in markdown. Students learn elementary programming concepts (loops, data structures, dataframes, ...) in Python. Moreover, it allows you to explain the economics and econometrics that you use to people who do not necessarily have a background in economics. For students with little or no background in programming this course may seem daunting. This course is developed in such a way that every student, who puts some effort into it, will acquire basic programming skills. y2-game.name: Micro 3: Game Theory
y2-game.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The course aims at introducing students to the fundamental tools and concepts of game theory, thus developing their capacity to reason formally and critically about strategic interdependence. Students learn to identify the incentives, constraints, and informational conditions that shape economic interactions, and to use appropriate analytical tools to evaluate the possible outcomes of such situations. The course further allows to strengthen students’ ability to connect abstract models to economic and societal questions. By constructing, solving, and interpreting strategic models, students develop transferable skills in analytical thinking, economic reasoning, and the assessment of policy-relevant problems involving incentives, information, and coordination. On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Use basic concepts and tools of game theory, in particular the different concepts of equilibria for games with perfect and imperfect information. Formulate the issues raised by moral hazard and adverse selection and build the related optimal contracts or screening and signaling schemes. Solve strategic communication models and interpret their insights. Relate the three types of imperfect information (hidden action, hidden type, hidden state of the world) to real life examples.
y2-game.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The course covers basic concepts of game theory and explores their applications in several contexts, with a particular emphasis on the role of information. The course is divided in different chapter, each covering a type of game, the related equilibrium concept and at least one relevant related application. For instance simultaneous, sequential and repeated games are discussed, as well as games of perfect and imperfect information. Applications include moral hazard and adverse selection. Specific attention is brought to discussing the real-life relevance and implication of the models discussed in class. Type of instructions 2-hour interactive lecture and 2-hour tutorial in the typical week. Recommended Prerequisites Microeconomics 1 and 2, Mathematics 1, and Statistics

y2-cycles.name: Macro 3: Business Cycles and Crises
y2-cycles.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The goal of this course is to further develop the student’s macroeconomic way of reasoning, with special attention for dynamic policy issues at an intermediate level. At the end of the course, the student can apply the dynamic aggregate supply and demand model to current topics and analyze the macroeconomic effects of fiscal and monetary policies, can explain and analyze how politicians can influence the economy based on their own preferences, possibly leading to socially suboptimal outcomes, can explain and analyze how governments can influence the economies of other member countries in a monetary union, can explain and analyze the real and monetary effects of economic crises, can make economically sensible team policy decisions in an interactive environment, report and defend the implemented policies, and criticize the decisions of others. Recommended Prerequisites: Macroeconomics 1, Macroeconomics 2, Mathematics 1, Microeconomics 1
y2-cycles.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Booms and recessions: static & dynamic aggregate supply and demand, fiscal and monetary policy, Currency unions: the European monetary system, monetary and fiscal policy in the Euro zone, Endogenous economic policy: political business cycles, policy games, time inconsistency trap, Economic crises: financial crises, lockdowns due to pandemics, stagflation, hysteresis.

y2-econometrics.name: Econometrics
y2-econometrics.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students: 1. Understand basic techniques of empirical economics, including linear regression and instrumental variables estimation. 2. Are able to apply these techniques using the software package R, in applied economic research leading to a term paper or a BSc thesis. 3. Are well-prepared to study more advanced topics in applied econometrics, such as the analysis of time series and panel data. 4. Are aware of pitfalls in interpreting results from econometric analyses.
y2-econometrics.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Description This course provides an introduction to econometric methods, with a strong emphasis on the application of these methods in applied economic research. In the first half of the course, students first acquire a basic understanding of the nature of empirical research and the possibilities and limitations of econometric methods. Then, they study the basics of one of econometrics’ key tools, linear regression analysis of cross-sectional data. Along the way, students are introduced to the software package R and econometric methods are illustrated with empirical examples and empirical exercises. In the second half of the course, more advanced topics, including regression analysis with heteroskedastic and autocorrelated data, causal inference, instrumental variables estimation, and simultaneous equations models are studied. In addition, students are guided in writing a small research paper in empirical economics. Format The course (6 ECTS) is taught in 14 weeks, with one 1h45m lecture and one 1h45m workshop session each week (sometimes we will call these workshop sessions "tutorials" or "computer labs"). The core material is presented in 9 videos and discussed in the lectures. The videos and slides are available at https://www.tobiasklein.ws/open-education under the heading "Econometrics (B.Sc.)". The workshop sessions teach students how to use the software package R for empirical work. They also review parts of the core material and deepen the understanding with empirical and other practical exercises and examples. Outline Weeks 1-7: Introduction and basics of regression analysis The first seven lectures cover the nature of econometrics and economic data (Chapter 1), the simple regression model (Chapter 2), multiple regression analysis: estimation (Chapter 3), multiple regression analysis: inference (Chapter 4), and a brief discussion of properties of the OLS estimator in large samples (optional reading: Chapter 5). A selection of topics from Chapters 6 and 7 (optional reading) is covered along the way. Weeks 8-14: Some advanced topics The last seven lectures cover heteroskedasticity (Chapter 8), aspects of time series analysis and autocorrelated errors (parts of Chapters 10 and 12), instrumental variables, simultaneous equations, and causal analysis (Chapters 15 and 16). Reading We will use a single text book, Jeffrey Wooldridge (2019), Introduction to Econometrics: A Modern Approach, 7 th edition, Cengage Learning. Students can also use recent earlier editions of this book, but are themselves responsible for sorting out any differences. The book Florian Heiss (2020): Using R for Introductory Econometrics , 2 nd edition nicely complements our course, but is not required reading. A html version is freely available at http://urfie.net/ . mcEmpirics We have bought a subscription for mcEmpirics. It nicely complements the course. You can use it at your own discretion. It's not mandatory and does not have an impact on your grade. There will be quizzes for each Chapter that we cover. Click here to get started: https://www.mcempirics.com/accounts/signup/qgyngprjolqcvkffowbxgha1bhwkergwwshyyd564eua40vyhapijtp2kax5qams Grading Students are expected to actively participate in all lectures and workshop sessions. The final grade is based on homework assignments (25%) and a final written exam (75%). Students can only pass the course if they pass the final exam (receive at least 55 percent of the points in the exam; otherwise the course grade is 1). The same is true for the resit exam. The homework assignments include a number of Canvas Quizzes. The final exam is a closed book exam. Students can bring (any) calculator, but communication devices (including internet-enabled calculators) are not allowed. Resit policy The final exam can be retaken once this academic year (for 75% of the grade). The homework assignments cannot be retaken during the year; the initial grade also contributes to the final grade for the resit (25%). Students who did not pass the course last (or in an earlier) year need to retake the entire course this year.

y2-trade.name: International Trade
y2-trade.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After completion of the course you are able to: Interpret core theories of international trade relevant to international business and policymaking. Apply these theories to real-world business and policy cases. Analyze the dilemmas and trade-offs faced by national and international policymakers. Develop and implement a quantitative trade model to generate calibrated predictions in response to external shocks. Formulate and communicate evidence-based policy advice under uncertainty, reflecting on assumptions, limitations, and the strategic use of analytical tools.
y2-trade.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Whereas in the first Bachelor year some macro aspects of international economics were discussed, the current course discusses some micro aspects, and, more precisely, international trade. The emphasis of the present course is on the determinants and effects of trade flows and of trade policy. The former part asks questions as: How can we explain the pattern of international trade, that is: Who exports what? And who gains from international trade and who loses? In this framework we will discuss both the traditional explanations - assuming perfect competition - as well as the more modern theories that assume imperfect competition, based on economies of scale and on product differentiation on the one hand, and productivity differences, on the other (also known as firm heterogeneity). The latter part of the course, on trade policy, discusses the purposes and effects of various forms of trade policy. We will look here at the arguments for free trade vs. 'managed trade' and at reasons why governments use trade policy to protect locally based industries. Type of instructions Lectures and tutorials

y2-bigdata.name: The Political Economy of Big Data
y2-bigdata.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After completion of the course, you are able to: Explain how data differs from traditional commodities, and show how these differences shape the role of intermediaries and the dynamics of data markets. Apply models of political participation and belief formation to analyze the influence of social media on political outcomes and polarization. Identify and assess the potential risks associated with social media and AI use, including broader societal and geopolitical implications.
y2-bigdata.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } This course explores the societal and political implications of big data, with particular attention to the risks citizens face in the age of digital data. Drawing on the tools of political economy and microeconomics, the lectures examine the mechanisms through which digital data affects regulatory frameworks and politics. In addition, the course is designed to familiarize students with the approach and foundations of political economy. The course covers several interconnected themes. In particular, we begin by analyzing the data markets and how the distinct features of data shape intermediaries incentives and market dynamics. We then turn to the political sphere, focusing on how social media influences information flow, political participation, and belief formation. Finally, we consider emerging challenges linked to the rise of artificial intelligence, with a focus on societal risks and geopolitical implications. By combining formal and rigorous perspectives with timely debates, the course equips students with the analytical tools and critical perspectives necessary to understand and navigate the growing influence of big data on politics and society.

y2-competence.name: Competence Compass
y2-competence.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Upon successful completion of this course, you are able to: Critically evaluate one’s own competency levels, translate the insights into well-considered study or career choices, and reflect on this process. Make choices about which competencies to develop, take personal responsibility for doing so, and translate this, through dialogue with others, into concrete development actions. Find and select relevant academic information by distinguishing between types of information and conducting effective searches in the library catalogue and relevant library databases.
y2-competence.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Discovering already developed personal strengths and identifying growth paths is both exciting and essential. In this course, you assess your current level across a set of competencies and support your self-assessment with concrete evidence. A competence is the combination of knowledge, skills, and attitude that makes you effective in practice. It is valuable to better understand yourself and support your personal and professional development. In this course, you report via a portfolio on both your current competency levels and your personal development plan. The competences are divided into three clusters, and you choose from each cluster one competency, based on a diagnostic test. The clusters are: Resilience and self-regulation: 1) self-confidence, 2) setting and monitoring boundaries, 3) optimal balance study/work and personal development, 4) reflection on development and performance. Goal setting and performance: 5) working in a goal-oriented manner, 6) focusing attention, 7) planning, 8) process-oriented working, 9) performing under pressure. Problem solving and communication: 10) communicating, 11) making decisions, 12) problem-solving ability, 13) perseverance, 14) adaptability. This course is part of the bachelors Economics, Econometrics and Operations Research, Entrepreneurship and Business Innovation, and International Business Administration. The course is an online course in block 1 in Canvas with weekly deadlines and assignments.

y2-industrial.name: Micro 4: Industrial Economics
y2-industrial.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After successful completion of this course, students will be able to… Apply the relevant theoretical framework to analyze how firms with market power price their products to maximize profits and how they position their products when consumers differ in their preferred product characteristics (horizontal differentiation). Apply the relevant theoretical framework to determine the optimal way for a monopolist to price discriminate when facing several types of consumers, both from a neoclassical and behavioral economics perspective. Solve for the equilibrium of a static oligopoly game with quantity or price competition and determine the conditions under which collusion is sustainable in an infinitely repeated version of the game. Evaluate market structure by solving for, and discussing the welfare properties of, the equilibrium of an entry game, and by investigating the implications of mergers among horizontal competitors for profits, consumer surplus, and welfare. Apply the relevant theoretical framework to analyze the ability and incentives of firms to deter rivals from entering or to induce them to exit, and derive the implications of various contractual arrangements between firms and their suppliers or retailers (vertical contracts) for profits, consumer surplus, and welfare. Calculate firms’ incentives to invest in innovation, evaluate the welfare properties of equilibrium investment, and evaluate the effectives of government policies to promote innovation. Apply the relevant theoretical framework to analyze demand, adoption decisions, and competition in the presence of network effects.
y2-industrial.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In this course, we focus on how firms make decisions such as pricing, how much to produces, whether to enter a market, etc. In addition, we also consider government intervention and investigate if this can improve market outcomes. The goal is to provide the students with up-to-date knowledge about the essential issues in the field of industrial organization, and to equip the students with a consistent toolkit for analyzing and understanding these issues. The course blends the standard theoretical approach, viewing the firm as a rational decision maker, with empirical studies, and gives students real-life examples to help put the material in perspective. The topics covered are: Price discrimination Oligopoly Collusion Market structure Horizontal mergers Entry deterrence Vertical relations Product differentiation Innovation Networks Naivete-based price discrimination Monopsony Types of instruction The course consists of weekly lectures and (on average) bi-weekly tutorials. The lectures introduce the concepts and models. In tutorials, students discuss and solve practice questions to help them learn the material better and check their own understanding.

y2-growth.name: Macro 4: Economic Growth and Institutions
y2-growth.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Apply analytical frameworks to characterize the determinants of the process of economic growth. Analyze the role of factor accumulation and innovation in income level and growth differences across countries. Empirically investigate the contribution of differences in factor accumulation and productivity to income and growth differences across countries. Assess the role of institutions and geography as fundamental determinants of economic growth and prosperity in the long run. Apply analytical frameworks to study the interdependence between long-run economic prosperity and environmental quality. Produce reports that communicate in a clear manner findings from data analyses and from model simulations of alternative policy pathways.
y2-growth.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } General Description Why are some countries richer than others? Why have some economies been able to sustain high growth rates for decades, while others have stagnated? What are the fundamental factors which lead to substantial differences in living standards across countries? This course provides an overview of the theoretical and empirical tools of long-run macroeconomics that can be used to address these questions. In the course we further discuss the consistency of the assumptions and implications of theoretical economic growth models with historical evidence. Course format The course is composed of 3 interlinked parts. The first part presents the mechanics of economic growth through its proximate determinants: factor accumulation and productivity. The second part studies the role of innovation as engine of sustained economic growth. The third part discusses the fundamental determinants of economic growth: natural resources and institutions. The economic concepts underlying the process of modern economic growth are introduced and explained during the lectures. For this, various stylized models of economic growth are presented and analyzed. These models are dynamic, meaning that the time dimension features prominently and that the models produce the evolution of the variables of interest over time. The analysis of the models leverages this distinctive characteristic and differentiates between transitional and long-term outcomes. During the lectures, tutorials, and assessment activities, the theoretical framework is employed to evaluate the possible impacts of policies and shocks on the growth path of economies and the long-run level of per capita income and other outcomes of interest. Throughout the course, the assumptions and outcomes of the theoretical models are motivated and assessed by referring to relevant empirical evidence and historical case studies. The main textbook and complementary academic articles (announced via canvas) are the compulsory readings for this course. This is preparatory material for the lectures and the tutorials. Lectures: Are mainly devoted to introduce and interactively discuss the technical details of the compulsory material (theoretical models and empirical evidence). These discussions will be complemented with some specific cases and motivating evidence, which will partly discussed in class and partly left for own reading. Tutorials: Are intended as an opportunity to gain hands-on experience solving and analyzing the theoretical models by going over the weekly problem sets. Students are expected play an active role during the tutorials and prepare the problem sets in advance. The problem sets are not graded, but are important to facilitate the understanding of the material and are considered as exam preparation material.

y2-development.name: Development Economics
y2-development.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Interpret the key themes of development economics and analyze how these themes are operationalized in top academic papers Present and discuss academic papers, delivering clear presentations and providing critical, constructive feedback to an audience. Formulate well-grounded arguments in academic debates by engaging with key themes, relating them to the literature, and responding to peers’ arguments. Interpret commonly used statistical methods in empirical research (e.g., OLS, IV, RCTs, difference-in-differences) and formulate research hypotheses, select and apply appropriate methods, and conduct empirical analysis using data and statistical software. Critically assess the quality of academic studies, evaluating their statistical analyses and the underlying assumptions.
y2-development.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } The focus of this course will be on current topics in the development economics literature. We will cover both microeconomic and macroeconomic perspectives. Nevertheless, the main focus of the course will be on the microeconomic issues of development and poverty, as the macroeconomic perspective is studied in complementary courses. The course proposes an in-depth exploration into the most important issues of persistent world poverty. Questions such as the following are explored through lectures, discussions, readings, and presentations: Why poverty persists? How do we make schools work for poor citizens? How do we deal with the disease burden? What do the poor do for living? How do they manage their businesses? How do they finance themselves? Is micro finance useful or overrated? How do people make their decisions under extreme poverty? How institutions shape countries development? Students will be encouraged to actively participate during both lectures and tutorials. Tutorials will consist of (i) students’ presentations and (ii) questions/answers and debates. Course Meeting Times 12 Lectures: Each lecture divided in 2 blocks of 45 minutes 8 Tutorials: Each tutorial with students’ presentations, graded questions and answers sessions and debates. 1 Synthesis lecture with innovative ideas brought by you Required Prerequisites Students should have completed an introductory econometrics course and should have a basic knowledge of regression analysis, including ordinary least squares (OLS) and instrumental variables estimation.

y2-public.name: Public Sector Economics
y2-public.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Clarify why certain government interventions may or may not promote economic activity in various contexts. Analyze and discuss the underlying motives behind the implementation of specific policies. Assess the effectiveness of interventions and critically evaluate weaknesses in empirical studies related to policy evaluations.
y2-public.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } This course analyzes the role governments play in organizing economic activity. Topics covered include education, taxation, health insurance, pension insurance, and political economy. We will approach these topics from both a theoretical, as well as an empirical perspective. The language of instruction is English. Prerequisites Microeconomics 1, Microeconomics 2, Econometrics Recommended Most of the content will be accessible with the knowledge from Microeconomics 1 and 2, as well as Econometrics, but some materials may draw on other courses such as Intermediate Microeconomics and Macroeconomics 1 (and possibly further courses in the macroeconomics sequence). Refreshing the content from these courses at the appropriate time may be helpful.

y2-data-communication.name: Communicating Societal Problems with Data
y2-data-communication.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After successfully completing this course, the student: understands why some graphs and figures work well while others either fail to inform actively or mislead can independently produce data visualizations in R according to provided standards can explain a policy relevant economic problem with the aid of graphs and figures can write and orally present a policy report about a relevant economic problem can write with a clear and logical narrative and appropriate language can demonstrates a clear and suitable text structure, appropriate policy language and accurate source citations in APA format can responsibly use (scholarly) sources and Generative AI for writing products can convincingly convey a story using appropriate body language and clear and integrated visual support.
y2-data-communication.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In this course, students will learn and practice a combination of skills. They will also broaden their perspective on international economic policy issues and different institutions. The first part of the course is devoted to the practical analysis and presentation of real data, while also covering some material on the aesthetic and especially cognitive aspects of graphical perception and interpretation. For this, the programming language R will be used. The second part focuses on developing the communicative skills (including writing and presentation skills) of students. This component of the course will be taught by a Language Center instructor. The obtained skills will be applied in preparing and presenting the policy report, the individual assignment of this course. In the third part of the course, students will use their economic knowledge to individually work on a policy report discussing, with the help of data, a relevant economic policy issue in e.g. their country of origin, the EU, or a historically relevant issue. The policy report will be presented in the last two weeks of the course. NOTE: this course is only open to regular BSc Economics students!

y3-mobility.name: Study Abroad
y3-mobility.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } As a TiSEM bachelor student you can study at one of our partner universities abroad for one semester. The following rules apply with respect to the selection of the courses at the partner university: An exchange consists of 30 ECTS study load of which 24 ECTS must be in the Business / Economics domain. Only select bachelor level courses, Master level courses are not allowed for bachelor students. Languages and skills courses are not allowed (only ON TOP of 30 ECTS). Only English taught courses are allowed. Important: The selected courses should not overlap with the bachelor courses of your educational program at TiU. It depends on your bachelor if the exchange is part of your program or on top of program. Check the canvas page of your program; the rules above apply in al cases. Go to https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/students/studying/abroad for more information. You always need approval for the selected courses abroad; use the online request form OSIRIS Student to request approval well in advance.

y3-philosophy-history.name: Philosophy and History of Economic Thought
y3-philosophy-history.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: Analyze major economic thinkers within their historical, political, and cultural contexts to understand how these shape economic visions and contemporary debates. Assess the ethical assumptions and public responsibilities within economic theories, reflecting on the economist’s role in society and policymaking. Apply the three analytical dimensions—context, ideas, and social role—to interpret classical and lesser-known economic authors. Communicate economic ideas effectively through written and audio formats, engaging diverse audiences with clarity and purpose. Research and collaborate on historical and ethical questions in economic thought, reflecting on one’s analytical and communicative development.
y3-philosophy-history.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } This course provides a critical and historically informed examination of economic thought's evolution from its modern origins to the present day, emphasizing the ethical, philosophical, and societal aspects of economic ideas. These concepts, developed by classical and modern economists, transcend mere abstraction as they actively influence current discussions on inequality, policy, market dynamics, and the responsibilities of economists. By studying key authors and schools of thought, students will explore four foundational dimensions for each thinker: Historical, political, and cultural context: How their economic vision was influenced by their time and place. Key economic ideas: How these relate to their broader perspectives on human nature and society. Role of economists and economic policy: The ethical and social consequences of their theories. Literary and rhetorical style: Their methods of writing, arguing, and persuading. This course integrates intellectual history with ethical analysis and stylistic examination, providing students with the understanding necessary to grasp the evolution of economic ideas and their ongoing significance in tackling contemporary economic and social issues.

y3-competition.name: Competition Policy and Regulation
y3-competition.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: (i) solve some economic models relevant for competition policy and regulation analytically; (ii) use Python to program and numerically solve those models; (iii) interpret the outcomes of economic models in order to derive policy implications; (iv) clarify the relationship between competition laws, economic models and the outcomes of these models; (v) explain and apply the main concepts of competition policy and regulation.
y3-competition.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } In this course, we provide an overview of the economic theories underpinning modern competition policy and sectoral regulation. We do so by exposing those theories and illustrating them with examples and cases, but also by working out numerical examples which have to worked out (i.e. coded) using Python. Hence, beyond the primary (content) goal of mastering the economic foundations of two important forms of government intervention in the functioning of markets, the course has a secondary (skill) goal of learning the basics of that open programming language. Both skills may prove useful in your future career as an economic analyst or other occupations. Contents ∗ Introduction: basic economic concepts relevant for competition policy ∗ Agreements between Firms (Article 101). ∗ Vertical Agreements. ∗ Article 102: Abuse of a dominant position (two lectures). ∗ Mergers (4 lectures). ∗ Innovation. ∗ Regulation of a monopolist. ∗ Competition in health care markets. Type of instruction Webinar (DataCamp), video lectures and interactive lectures. Required Prerequisites Microeconomics 1 or equivalent Mathematics 1 or equivalent Industrial Economics or equivalent Recommended Prerequisites Information Economics or equivalent

y3-environment.name: Environmental Economics
y3-environment.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } After having completed this course, you are able to identify the general (underlying) causes of environmental problems, including (renewable) resource depletion and climate change; list the criteria on the basis of which the various environmental policy instruments (taxes, quotas, voluntary agreements) can be evaluated, and identify the key considerations that determine optimality; identify why the practice of environmental regulation may differ from the theoretically preferred design; understand the causes, consequences, and possible policies to address climate change.
y3-environment.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Course description Natural capital is the basis for all economic activity since the economy is embedded in nature. Depleting natural capital must ultimately hurt the economy. Yet in the short run and from a narrow private point of view, resources and polluting production might generate market share, income, and profits. This tension between planet and profits is at the heart of many environmental problems, like the climate problem and loss of biodiversity. At the same time, technical change in electrical vehicles and solar panel have lowered the cost of a transition to a cleaner economy. These two examples show that economics can contribute to both explaining environmental problems and solving them. The course helps you analyze the economic roots of environmental problems and think about incentives that help solve the problems. Environmental and resource economics studies the optimal management of nature and natural resources; it integrates resources and environmental pollution into economic analysis. The aim of this course is to provide students with key insights regarding the nature of environmental problems and how environmental policy should be designed. The lectures offer a treatment of modern economic theories and methods to study the relationship between natural resources, environmental quality, economic structure and environmental policy. As a student in this course, you will develop a thorough understanding of key economic, environmental, and ethical aspects of environmental problems, and of the link between theory, methods, and empirical analysis. The course consists of two parts. In part 1 (week 1-6), we discuss the fundamental causes of environmental problems and economically sound remedies. The concept of “externality” is central here – it explains why inefficient and undesirable use of natural resources takes place and gives a powerful perspective on how to solve these problems. We then move to policy instruments. What policy instruments are available for policy implementation? What are the pros and cons of each of them? Which policy instrument works best under different forms of imperfect information? To assess how we can quantify environmental damages and prevention costs as a basis for environmental policy, we develop a method for cost-benefit analysis, with a focus on the valuation of environmental costs and benefits. We introduce and compare two main branches of valuation methods are discussed, hedonic pricing and stated preferences. To analyze the impact of uncertainty about costs and benefits, our analysis builds on the concept of option value. We conclude this part with an analysis of the interaction between international trade and environmental policy: is trade good for the environmental, and if not what are good policies to reconcile trade and the environment? In part 2 (week 7-16), we turn to the depletion of natural resources and environmental problems over time. Fundamental question we ask are the following. Are we depleting resources like oil and minerals too fast? What threatens the world fish stocks, forests, and other natural resources and what are economically sound policies to preserve nature? Is economic growth the enemy of biodiversity and nature preservation? And last but not least, what is the economics behind climate change? Did we wait too long and how fast should we make a transition to a carbon neutral economy? To analyze the economics of natural resources, we introduce renewable and non-renewable resource theory. For renewable resources, like fish, the focus is on the difference between optimal management and open access to the resource. For non-renewable resources, like oil, the focus is on the optimal extraction path and the conditions for growth, in case the resource is essential for production. The economics of climate change brings everything together: in our growing world economy, the use of fossil non-renewable resources and deforestation has caused greenhouse gases to cumulate in the atmosphere -- a stock pollution problem leading to global warming. Type of instruction One lecture and one tutorial per week, for 13 weeks in total.

y3-thesis.name: BSc Thesis Economics
y3-thesis.outcomes: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } A Bachelor thesis is the final component of a Bachelor degree and provides students with the opportunity to show that they have gained the necessary skills and knowledge in order to apply and write about economic ideas in a coherent, clear way. It provides the opportunity for students to plan, complete, interpret, and report research. At the end of a successful completion of the BSc thesis component, students will be able to: Formulate and motivate a research question*, Formulate a hypothesis based on a thorough, independent, literature review, Formulate and motivate a research strategy including a research method based on the literature review, available time frame, and available data*, Analyze their findings and the implications with respect to the literature review, Formulate an independent argument, appropriate to and based on the chosen method, to answer the research question, Communicate their research and findings to an academic audience in English, and Present their research to an academic audience in English. * The research question and method may be based on a research project developed by a supervisor or suggested by a supervisor.
y3-thesis.contentAndEntry: body { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } table { font-size: 9pt; font-family: Arial } Students have one opportunity to write their thesis in each academic year. Students may do so in Fall semester, starting in late August, or Spring semester, starting in late January. Most students will start their thesis in the Spring semester. If a student does not successfully defend his/her thesis by the end of a thesis period, he/she must start another thesis on a new topic in the same semester of the next academic year. There should be at least one semester between subsequent attempts to write a thesis. The following requirements apply for a student in order to be assigned a supervisor and write a thesis: Required prerequisites must be obtained (see below), Enrollment, via OSIRIS, to the Canvas course page is mandatory, In addition to Canvas enrollment, students must register on time in the thesis system using an appropriate form. The thesis proposal must be approved on time for the student to submit and defend a thesis. If the research proposal is not approved on time, the student must begin with a new topic in the next thesis cycle. Information about the timing and organization of the thesis is published on Canvas. Required Prerequisites To participate in the Bachelor thesis, students should have: passed the first year skills requirements of the Bachelor program, and earned a sufficient amount of ECTS credits at Tilburg University (including approved courses during an exchange period). Students starting in the 6th semester of their Bachelor study need at least 120 ECTS credits, while students starting in the 7th semester or later need at least 138 ECTS credits.

findings: Current public curriculum and adopted Economics cohort table agree on 180 EC. Year one is nine six-credit subjects and two three-credit programming units. Year two is nine six-credit subjects plus two three-credit units. Year three has a thirty-credit first-semester window and thirty Spring credits. Zero-credit GROW is extracurricular. No EOR 144-credit/ISL rule is imported into Economics.

First adopted mobility option is exchange, selected independently of UCR fit. Thirty approved credits must be bachelor-level English subjects, at least twenty-four business/economics, nonoverlapping with home study and excluding language/skills courses. Host and approved subjects remain open within those conditions; internship-plus-elective and minors remain mutually exclusive alternatives rather than extra units. No unsupported host or specific partner package is invented.

The twelve-credit restricted Spring group must be instantiated. First two adopted menu entries are Competition Policy and Regulation and Environmental Economics, both six credits. They replace the generic elective component. Competition requires first microeconomics, mathematics and Industrial Economics, all completed earlier. The public page orders some electives differently; adopted cohort menu controls the neutral tie-break. The three other elective menu subjects are not added.

Competition specifically combines economic models, Python, agreements/mergers/dominance and regulation. Environmental Economics studies externalities, resource depletion, policy instruments, cost-benefit valuation, resource dynamics and climate policy. Required Game Theory has equilibrium/information, moral hazard/adverse selection and strategic communication, not behavioural experiments alone. Political Economy of Big Data models data intermediaries and political participation/beliefs; it is not generic data science.

The Economics thesis is an English written and presented research project with research question, independent literature review, hypothesis, research method, findings and argument. Catalogue and cohort table require at least 120 EC from semester six or 138 from semester seven, including first-year skills. R/Python skills are completed in year one; all 120 earlier credits plus thirty exchange give 150 before the Spring thesis. Timely Canvas/OSIRIS and thesis-system registration and approved proposal are explicit requirements. A failed attempt requires a new topic and at least one intervening semester. No extra credits, thesis word count or unrelated programme prerequisite is invented.

Philosophy/Science/Free Markets has current substantive outcomes in reasoning errors, scientific method, distributive justice and the place of markets. Its detailed assessment prose retains old 2018 dates; these are not used as current deadlines or timetable facts. Philosophy and History of Economic Thought is a different required unit on thinkers, context, ethics and social roles. Source metadata/content distinctions remain internal.
